column3: It directly states that other gods are adopted in the expectation that they will bring help.
It distinguishes the judgment-day failure of unpermitted intercession from help that depends wholly on divine permission.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, extending the focus from idols to every claimed support.
It explicitly joins the absence of helpers besides God with inability to defend oneself.
The immediate judgment setting frames why the claimed helpers of the following verses are tested.
Its challenge exposes the collapse of mutual aid, but does not identify the failed objects of worship.
Human resistance to oppression uses self-defense differently and adds little to the failed-idol claim.
The same scene admits the absence of intercessors, adding a distinct failed-mediation dimension.
God as guide and helper for prophets supplies a positive contrast, not the focus's failed intermediaries.
It denies a protector or helper besides God against divine will, though the setting is broader than idol worship.
The near-day scene denies an obeyed intercessor and sharpens the judgment context of failed mediation.
It makes a claim to divinity besides God answerable to punishment, but not the particular test of help.
The coming-punishment question has only a broad judgment connection to the focus.
The exposure of Hell is immediate narrative context for the interrogation about worshiped beings.
Divine help to messengers is a positive aid claim, distant from whether false gods can help.
It directly tests whether those called besides God can remove harm or withhold mercy.
The lack of an intimate friend adds the collapse of close human support in the same judgment scene.
It states that no patron can avail another or receive help on the Day, a close but less idol-specific parallel.
Its warning of the divine command arriving contributes only general eschatological background.
It explicitly calls the powerless worshiped beings alleged intercessors, directly explaining the false expectation behind the focus.
It identifies calling on what can neither harm nor benefit as manifest error, closely paralleling the failed help claim.
The verse concerns resentment of God's aid rather than reliance on false helpers.
The wish to return follows the failure of advocates in the same scene, showing its irreversible consequence.
A prophet's prayer for help identifies God as addressee but adds little after the stronger direct contrasts.
It challenges those invoked besides God to show creative authority, supplying a basis for their inability to help.
The immediate question whether the idols benefit or harm is the functional test developed by the focus.
Human action as a means of divine aid is not about alternative worshiped helpers.
At death, the invoked beings are sought and found absent, a judgment-day enactment of failed reliance.
Angelic prayer for believers is a permitted mediation scene but only indirectly clarifies the focus.
It says both acquisitions and protectors besides God will not avail, broadening the failure beyond a single idol.
The conflict outcome does not clarify the status of claimed divine helpers.
The opening question of Ibrahim's idol inquiry supplies the narrative source of the focus's later test.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, but repeats an already established general proposition.
It nearly states the focus verbatim: those invoked cannot help their callers or themselves.
The uselessness of wealth and children establishes the same scene's wider collapse of worldly support.
A separate punishment before the final one does not clarify false helpers or self-defense.
It repeats the dual inability to help worshipers or themselves, but adds little beyond 7:197.
The list of communities judged by God offers only broad judgment background.
Lack of a helper after divine curse is a remote instance without worship or mediation.
It denies protectors who can help besides God, adding the loss of any path after misguidance.
The confession of worshiping idols identifies the objects whose efficacy is questioned in the focus.
Broken political promises of assistance are a social analogy, not a claim about false gods.
Return to God after death does not address help, worship, or mediation.
Pilgrimage benefits and remembrance do not illuminate the failure of claimed helpers.
It assigns victory to God, but its military means do not clarify worshiped intermediaries.
The prophet's accountability before God is only a distant aid-related contrast.
The immediate question whether idols hear their callers begins the proof that they cannot aid them.
The fragile-house image illustrates why taking protectors besides God cannot provide real protection.
It explicitly says alleged gods cannot help themselves, directly matching one half of the focus.
The invoked beings disappear when questioned in the Hereafter, extending the same failed-dependency scene.
It defines God as the decisive source of victory, a positive contrast to reliance on powerless helpers.
It joins inability even to rise with inability to secure help, but without the worship dimension.
Inherited practice explains why the idol attachment persists despite its failure.
The boast of collective victory is only a general false confidence in self-help.
A powerful man's supporters and self-rescue fail, providing a concrete non-idol parallel to the twofold failure.
It states the ineffectiveness of intercession, but does not distinguish permitted from falsely claimed mediation.
It questions what army could help besides the Merciful, applying the focus's test to collective power.
Questions of control over divine stores do not directly concern help or worshiped beings.
Ibrahim's direct question about what they worship sets up the later inquiry into whether those beings can help.
It repeats the absence of protector and helper besides God without adding a new setting.
It warns against leaning on wrongdoers because no protectors besides God can then help.
The question who can save from God's might challenges political power as a failed protector.
The promise of mighty help to the Prophet is a positive aid statement with limited relevance.
It denies any remover besides God at the decisive event, a close sovereignty parallel.
The inclusion of ancient fathers explains inherited worship but is redundant after 26:74.
Divine victory at Badr is a remote positive example of help.
It directly rejects seeking fabricated gods besides God, supporting the focus's object-of-worship critique.
God as the excellent protector and helper provides the affirmative alternative to the failed allies.
The powerless ownership of those invoked besides God is relevant but less direct than prior incapacity texts.
The disappearance of former generations does not clarify worshiped helpers.
Ibrahim declares the worshiped beings enemies except the Lord, drawing the conclusion of their failure.
The lack of helpers for wrongdoers is too general to add to the established pattern.
It directs those worshiped besides God to Hell, supplying an afterlife consequence rather than an aid test.
The questioners in gardens add no usable connection on their own.
Misguidance without helpers is a broad moral consequence, not an analysis of false gods.
Those who find no helpers besides God after destruction enact the focus's failed-rescue claim.
The immediate question asking where the worshiped beings are is the direct lead-in to 26:93.
It contrasts following revelation with taking protectors besides God, giving the practical alternative.
It explicitly asks why gods adopted as means of nearness did not help and says they vanished.
Followers ask their leaders to remove a share of the Fire, showing human mediation also fails in the same judgment pattern.
Unsupported worship and the absence of any helper for wrongdoers connect false devotion with abandonment.
The general denial of protector and helper besides God adds no new angle.
The worshiped beings and their followers are cast into Hell, the immediate outcome of their failed reliance.
Its denial of intercession and help is a broader judgment rule already represented more directly.
Idol-based mutual affection turns to mutual denial and curse, showing social bonds built on idols collapse.
The confession of abandoning prayer supplies a cause within the judgment scene where intercession later proves ineffective.
It directly asks why people worship what controls neither harm nor benefit, closely explaining the focus.
The late uselessness of belief is general eschatological background only.
The gathering of Iblis's forces completes the condemned assembly around the failed worshipers.
The nearness of God's help in trial is a remote positive contrast.
Household eating permissions have no material connection to the focus.
God's support through believers is a positive communal-aid example, not false mediation.
The statement that God clarifies signs has no specific link to the focus.
Helping God and messengers concerns faithful action rather than the incapacity of false gods.
Military preparation does not clarify the claimed ability of worshiped beings to help.
A claim of special friendship with God is not about other-than-God helpers.
The bare reference to sinners supplies no independent explanatory content.
The denial of help on the Day reinforces the focus's irreversible judgment setting.
Night prayer, charity, and easing obligations do not address the focus's failed helpers.
Mutual aid among believers is a legitimate social support relation, only a distant contrast.
It states that the adopted gods cannot help their worshipers, directly completing 36:74's expectation of help.
Those invoked cannot hear or answer their callers and will deny the association on the Day of Resurrection.
The beings called besides God cannot remove harm or transfer it, directly testing their claimed efficacy.
In distress at sea all invoked beings vanish from reliance except God, a concrete crisis test of the focus.
It rejects calling on what can neither benefit nor harm besides God, directly paralleling the focus's failed aid.
It challenges associating beings that create nothing and cannot create, supplying a basis for their incapacity.
Calling the false objects to guidance produces no response, reinforcing their inability to act for callers.
Those invoked besides God are servants like their callers, so invocation tests rather than establishes their power.
Their lack of hearing, sight, and grasp exposes the incapacity behind their claimed protective role.
At judgment the alleged partners dissociate themselves from the worshipers, dissolving the claimed relation.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, directly undermining their supposed help.
They worship beings besides God that possess no provision, showing a lack of independent power.
It directly asks why they worship what neither benefits nor harms them besides God.
The adopted gods create nothing, are created, and control neither harm nor benefit, death nor life.
It identifies worship of what neither benefits nor harms as a rejection of the true Lord.
The idols worshiped besides God cannot provide sustenance, further specifying their dependence and failure.
The alleged beings besides God own not even an atom and have no share or supporting role in dominion.
Intercession has effect only after divine permission, supplying the necessary boundary to false advocacy.
It records the claim that protectors besides God bring nearness, directly exposing the intermediary rationale.
It challenges taking intercessors besides God even when they possess nothing and understand nothing.
It assigns all intercession to God, resolving the claim of autonomous mediators.
Those invoked besides God cannot judge anything, denying them decisive authority.
Those invoked besides God do not possess intercession except under the stated witness condition.
Nothing is more astray than calling on one who will not answer until the Day and is heedless of the call.
Those called besides God become enemies and deny the worship when people are gathered.
The dispute in Hell begins the immediate aftermath of the failed worship and aid claims.
The worshipers confess they were in manifest error, interpreting the failed reliance as misguidance.
They identify the error as equating their worshiped beings with the Lord of the worlds.
They attribute their being led astray to misleaders, adding the human transmission of the failed attachment.
